standard.title: Law-making processes
standard.description: the characteristics of laws and how laws are made in Australia through parliaments (statutory law) and through the courts (common law)
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Constitution, the rule of law and the court system (AC9HC7K03). They understand that democratic systems have structures and checks. The gap this descriptor fills is specifically how law is made — the characteristics that define a law and the two distinct sources (parliament and courts) through which Australian law is created.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the characteristics of laws in Australia and how laws are made through both parliamentary processes (statutory law) and through the courts (common law), including the role of delegated legislation and the relationship between parliament and the courts.

nodes.label: Characteristics of laws
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the key characteristics of laws in Australia — that they reflect society's values, are enforceable, are known, clear and understood, and are relatively stable.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least three characteristics of a law and explain why each characteristic matters for a functioning legal system.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the full set of characteristics of laws — reflecting society's values, being enforceable, being known and understood, and being relatively stable — and explain the function of each characteristic in maintaining a just and workable legal system.
wider: Examine a case where a law failed to meet one of its characteristics (e.g. a law that was unclear, widely ignored, or no longer reflected community values) and analyse the consequences
Investigate how community values have changed over time in ways that have prompted changes to Australian laws — with a specific example
Question whether current laws always meet the characteristic of reflecting society's values by examining a contested area of law from different perspectives
nodes.hinge_reason: The characteristics of laws are the evaluative framework used throughout this descriptor and K04. If students do not understand what makes something a law and why those features matter, they cannot analyse whether specific types of law (statutory, common, delegated, customary) satisfy or fail those characteristics. This conceptual foundation underpins the rest of the unit.

response_modes.reason: Students often treat the characteristics of laws as a list to memorise rather than as a functional framework. Invest in unpacking why each characteristic matters — what goes wrong when it is absent.

success_criteria: Can list and describe at least three characteristics of laws
Can explain why at least two of those characteristics are necessary for a just and workable legal system

nodes.label: Two sources of law: statute and common law
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the two chief sources of Australian law — parliament (statute law) and courts (common law) — and explain how each source creates law.
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish between statute law and common law, explaining how each is made and giving one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the two chief sources of Australian law, explain the law-making processes for each (parliament passing Acts; courts making decisions that set precedent), and analyse a case study that illustrates the operation of both statute and common law.
wider: Investigate a landmark common law case in Australian legal history and explain how the court's decision became law and whether it was later codified in statute
Examine how courts interpret statutes — what happens when parliament's law is ambiguous and courts must determine its meaning
Compare the speed and flexibility of common law development versus parliamentary statute-making in responding to new social or technological issues
nodes.hinge_reason: The distinction between statute and common law is foundational for K04, which requires students to understand multiple types of law including customary law. Conflating the two sources — or not understanding that courts make law through precedent — blocks meaningful engagement with how the Australian legal system operates as a whole.

response_modes.reason: Abstract law-making processes become meaningful through concrete cases. Widening across real examples of statute and common law — including landmark cases — prevents students from holding purely procedural understandings.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The interaction between statute and common law is rich pedagogically because it shows the legal system as dynamic rather than fixed. Case studies — particularly landmark common law cases — allow students to see how courts respond to gaps in statute and how the two sources interact over time.
success_criteria: Can explain how statute law is made, identifying the role of parliament
Can explain how common law is made, identifying the role of courts and the concept of precedent
Can distinguish the two sources in a specific legal example

nodes.label: Delegated legislation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how delegated (subordinate) legislation works — that governments can make rules under authority granted by an Act of parliament without parliament voting on each rule directly.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what delegated legislation is and give one example of where it is used.
nodes.typical_width: Explain that delegated legislation (also called subordinate legislation) is not made directly by parliament but operates under authority granted by a parliamentary Act — giving examples such as regulations, by-laws and statutory instruments — and explain why this mechanism exists and how parliament retains oversight of it.
wider: Investigate a specific example of delegated legislation (e.g. health regulations, road rules) and trace the Act of parliament that authorises it
Examine how the houses of parliament can disallow delegated legislation and why this oversight mechanism matters for democratic accountability
Investigate how extensive delegated legislation is in practice — examining how much of the regulatory law Australians encounter is delegated rather than directly parliamentary

response_modes.reason: Delegated legislation confuses students because it looks like executive action but derives its authority from parliament. Invest in explaining the chain of authority — Act → delegation → regulation — rather than just labelling it.

success_criteria: Can explain what delegated legislation is and why it exists
Can describe how parliament maintains oversight of delegated legislation

nodes.label: Cultural and social perspectives on law
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can question whether laws are affected by different cultural or social perspectives, using First Nations Australians as a key example of how cultural perspective intersects with law-making.
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example of how a cultural or social perspective has influenced or been in tension with Australian law.
nodes.typical_width: Examine whether and how Australian laws reflect or fail to reflect diverse cultural and social perspectives — with particular focus on First Nations Australians as a group whose legal traditions and social perspectives have frequently been in tension with statute and common law.
wider: Investigate a specific example where First Nations Australian cultural perspectives have influenced or challenged Australian statute or common law (e.g. land rights, customary practices, cultural heritage protection)
Examine how social change — such as changing attitudes to marriage equality or drug policy — has driven legal change, and analyse the lag between social perspectives and legislative change
Investigate how multicultural Australia's diverse religious and cultural communities interact with civil and criminal law — where tensions arise and how they are managed

response_modes.reason: This node has genuine width — multiple distinct cultural and social perspectives can be examined. Widening across First Nations perspectives, multicultural perspectives and changing social values shows students that law is not culturally neutral.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Examining law through multiple cultural perspectives — particularly First Nations perspectives — is substantively important for Australian civic literacy and is explicitly named in the elaborations. Width here produces students who can critically question the neutrality of law, not just describe how it is made.
success_criteria: Can give a specific example of how cultural or social perspectives have influenced or been in tension with Australian law
Can explain why the law-making process may not automatically reflect the perspectives of all groups in a diverse society

nodes.label: Relationship between parliament and the courts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the relationship between parliament and the courts as law-making bodies, including that parliament is supreme but courts interpret statute and can fill gaps through common law.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one key aspect of the relationship between parliament and the courts as law-making bodies.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the relationship between parliament and the courts — that parliament is the supreme law-making body but courts interpret statutes, develop common law in areas where statute is silent, and review executive action. Explain how this interaction maintains the rule of law.
wider: Investigate a specific case where a court's interpretation of a statute led parliament to amend the legislation in response
Examine the role of the High Court of Australia in interpreting the Constitution and how this can limit what parliament can do
Investigate judicial review — what courts can and cannot do when reviewing government action, and why this matters for the rule of law

response_modes.reason: This node integrates statute law, common law, delegated legislation and the characteristics of laws into a coherent picture of how Australia's law-making system operates. Ensure the synthesis is explicit — that students can explain how the whole system fits together.

success_criteria: Can explain the key distinction between parliament and the courts as law-making bodies — that parliament legislates and courts interpret and develop common law
Can explain how the relationship between parliament and courts contributes to the rule of law in Australia
